progressionInfo.name: IV-I Plagal Cadence
progressionInfo.subtitle: The gentle resolution that closes hymns, seals gospel songs, and adds a sense of peaceful finality - the plagal cadence moves from subdominant to tonic without dominant tension, delivering calm arrival rather than dramatic resolution.

properties.label: IV (Subdominant)
properties.value: Warm, open sound that gently departs from home without creating dominant tension

properties.label: I (Tonic)
properties.value: The point of rest and resolution - home base where the cadence settles

properties.label: Relationship
properties.value: A soft, tension-free resolution - the subdominant descends to the tonic without leading-tone pull

properties.label: Interval
properties.value: Root movement of a perfect fourth downward (F down to C) or perfect fifth upward

properties.label: Why It Works
properties.value: IV and I share common tones and the motion avoids the tritone found in V7-I, producing a calm, hymn-like sense of closure

examples.label: Common Tone
examples.value: C is shared between both chords, anchoring the gentle resolution

chordDiagrams.title: IV-I in C Major
practiceNotes: Start on F major and resolve to C major - listen for the calm, settled feeling
Keep your 1st finger barring fret 1 on F, then release into the open C shape
Play F for 2 beats, then let C ring for 2 beats to hear the plagal resolution
Try singing 'A-men' over the F-C change to internalize the cadence

chordDiagrams.title: IV-I in G Major
practiceNotes: C to G is one of the most beginner-friendly plagal cadences on guitar
The ring finger can remain on the 3rd fret as a pivot between both shapes
Strum C for a full measure, then resolve to G and let it sustain
This key is excellent for accompanying vocal 'Amen' endings

advancedApplications.title: Common Variations
advancedApplications.description: Ways to expand the plagal cadence framework:
items: IV-I as a song ending tag after an authentic cadence (V-I then IV-I)
IVMaj7-IMaj7 for a lush, jazz-influenced plagal resolution (FMaj7 to CMaj7)
iv-I (minor plagal cadence) using Fm to C for a bittersweet, cinematic color
IV-I with added 9ths and suspensions for modern worship and ambient textures
IV5-I5 power chord version for a rock-style plagal ending

advancedApplications.title: Key Transposition
items: C Major: F - C
G Major: C - G
D Major: G - D
E Major: (barred A shape) - E
F Major: Bb - F

advancedApplications.title: Rhythm & Feel Ideas
advancedApplications.description: The plagal cadence adapts to many musical styles:
items: Slow whole-note sustain for hymn and choral endings - let each chord breathe
Gentle arpeggiated fingerpicking for introspective singer-songwriter resolutions
Gospel shuffle with rhythmic anticipation on the IV chord before settling on I
Ambient swells with volume knob or tremolo picking for cinematic fade-to-rest
Layered vocal harmonies singing 'Amen' over the IV-I for full choral effect

examples.title: The "Amen" Cadence in Hymns
examples.description: Nearly every traditional hymn ends with a IV-I plagal cadence sung as 'Amen'
examples.detail: The congregation sings 'A-' on the IV chord and '-men' on the I chord, creating the most recognized cadence in Western sacred music

examples.title: "Let It Be" (Ending) - The Beatles
examples.description: The famous C-F-C ending gesture is a plagal cadence in C major
examples.detail: McCartney's gospel-influenced songwriting uses the IV-I resolution to give the song its sense of peaceful acceptance and closure

examples.title: Gospel & Worship Music Tradition
examples.description: The plagal cadence is the harmonic backbone of gospel endings
examples.detail: From traditional spirituals to modern worship, the IV-I resolution provides a sense of divine peace and completion that the stronger V-I cannot match

examples.title: "Creep" (Ending) - Radiohead
examples.description: The song's final chord change uses a plagal-like resolution for emotional weight
examples.detail: The subdominant-to-tonic motion gives the ending a wistful, unresolved-yet-settled quality

examples.title: Classic Rock Song Endings
examples.description: Many rock songs add a IV-I tag after the final chorus for a definitive close
examples.detail: Bands from The Who to Led Zeppelin use the plagal cadence as a final punctuation mark before the last sustained chord

examples.title: Film & TV Scoring
examples.description: Composers use the plagal cadence for scenes of resolution, redemption, and peace
examples.detail: The gentler quality of IV-I (compared to V-I) signals emotional settling rather than dramatic triumph - perfect for quiet, meaningful moments

practiceCategories.title: Cadence Recognition
items: Play V-I (G to C) then IV-I (F to C) back to back and compare the resolution quality
Practice identifying plagal cadences in hymns, gospel songs, and pop recordings
Play the IV chord for 4 beats, then resolve to I and sustain - notice the calm arrival
Try the plagal cadence in C major (F-C), G major (C-G), and D major (G-D)
Record yourself playing IV-I and V-I cadences, then listen back to hear the difference

practiceCategories.title: Chord Transitions
items: Alternate F to C every 4 beats at 60 BPM, focusing on clean transitions
Speed up to 2-beat changes, keeping the resolution smooth and unhurried
Practice the F barre chord shape until every string rings clearly before resolving
Work on pivot fingers: keep the index finger anchored when moving from F to C
Try the same transitions in G major (C to G) with the ring finger as pivot

practiceCategories.title: Creative Application
items: Add a IV-I tag to the end of any song you already know for a peaceful conclusion
Write a short 4-bar phrase ending with F-C and notice how it closes the idea
Experiment with the minor plagal cadence: play Fm to C and compare the mood
Layer the IV-I cadence with different dynamics - try pianissimo for a whispered ending
Record a loop of I-IV-V-I and then add a IV-I tag at the end for extra closure

notatedExercises.title: Exercise 1: Basic Plagal Cadence in C Major
notatedExercises.description: Practice the fundamental IV-I resolution with sustained chords in C major:
practiceNotes: Hold F major for 4 beats, then resolve to C major for 4 beats
Let the C chord ring fully and listen for the sense of peaceful arrival
Sing 'A-men' (F on 'A-', C on '-men') to feel the cadence in your voice
Repeat until the resolution feels natural and the F chord is clean on every string

notatedExercises.title: Exercise 2: Gospel Plagal Cadence in G Major
notatedExercises.description: Practice the plagal resolution with a gospel feel using C to G in open position:
practiceNotes: Play C major (IV) with a gentle strum for 2 beats, then resolve to G major (I) for 2 beats
Add a slight ritardando (slowing down) on the IV chord before resolving to I
Try adding a bass walk-down from C to G: C note, B note, then land on G chord
Use this cadence to end any progression you practice today

notatedExercises.title: Exercise 3: Plagal Cadence with Extended Chords
notatedExercises.description: Enrich the IV-I cadence using major 7th voicings for a lush, modern sound:
practiceNotes: Play FMaj7 (IV) resolving to CMaj7 (I) in C major for a jazz-influenced plagal sound
Let each chord sustain for a full measure so the extended harmonies ring out
Compare the sound of FMaj7-CMaj7 to the basic F-C cadence and note the added warmth
Use this voicing as a sophisticated ending tag for ballads and jazz standards

sections.title: Scale Degrees
items: IV (F): 4th degree - Subdominant, a warm departure that sets up the resolution
I (C): 1st degree - Tonic, the home chord and ultimate resting point
Root movement by perfect 4th downward (F down to C) or perfect 5th upward
Unlike V-I, the IV chord contains no leading tone that pulls to the tonic
This absence of tension creates a floating, peaceful quality unique to the plagal cadence

sections.title: Why IV-I Feels Gentle, Not Dramatic
items: The IV chord shares a common tone with I (C appears in both F major and C major)
No tritone interval exists between IV and I (unlike the V7-I authentic cadence)
The resolution feels like settling or descending rather than snapping into place
The lack of leading-tone tension makes IV-I ideal for peaceful, reverent endings

sections.title: Common Tones (F and C major)
items: F major (F-A-C) resolves to C major (C-E-G)
C is the common tone shared between both chords, providing continuity
A moves down to G (whole step) - smooth descending voice leading
F moves down to E (half step) - the smoothest possible resolution
All voices move by step or stay put, producing extremely smooth voice leading

sections.title: Plagal vs. Authentic Cadence
items: Authentic cadence (V-I) has the leading tone pulling up a half step to the tonic root
Plagal cadence (IV-I) lacks this leading tone, so resolution is softer and less urgent
The plagal cadence is often used after an authentic cadence as a final 'Amen' tag
In classical theory, IV-I alone is considered a weaker cadence - but in gospel and pop it stands powerfully on its own
